source_text: Ὅσῳ γὰρ εὐσεβείᾳ τε καὶ δόξῃ διαφέρειν τὸν ἄνδρα ἐγίνωσκε, τοσούτῳ καὶ τὴν νίκην ἑαυτῷ περιφανεστέραν ἑώρα καὶ λαμπροτέραν, εἰ τούτου κρατή σειεν. Ἐκείνως μὲν γὰρ Χριστιανῶν μόνον ὑπάρχειν κρατεῖν, οὕτω δὲ καὶ φιλοσοφίας αὐτῆς, καὶ λόγων. Καὶ τὴν γλῶσσαν περιελεῖν πρότερον, εἶτα ἀφώνους ἀπαγαγεῖν καὶ ἀλόγους τοὺς ὑπ' ἐκείνης ἐρειδομένους, ἀρίστης εἶναι στρατηγίας ἐνόμιζεν· οὐκ ὀρθῶς μὲν, οὐδὲ εὐσεβῶς ταῦτα διανοού μενος, οὐ μὴν παντάπασιν ἀλογίστως, πρός γε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ βούλησιν καὶ ἐπιχείρησιν· ἔδειξε δὲ τὸ ἔργον. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἅπασαν προσβολήν τε καὶ πεῖραν ἀνδρικῶς τε καὶ γενναίως ἀποσεισάμενος, ὥσπερ τις πέτρα παράλιος κυμάτων ἐπιδρομὰς, τέλος ἐξορίαν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ κατακρίνεται· οὐ τὸ καθ' ἑαυτὸν ἔστερξεν ὁ γεννάδας, οὐδὲ ἠγάπα σωζόμενος· οὐδὲ ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι μᾶλλον τὴν ἀτιμίαν ἐνόμιζεν, ἢ ψυχῆς κίνδυνον τὴν ἡσυχίαν, καὶ τὸ περιορᾷν τοὺς ἄλλους τῷ καιρῷ κινδυνεύοντας, οὐκ ὄντος τοῦ παιδοτριβοῦντος, καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἀγῶνα θαῤῥύνοντος. Οὐ γὰρ μικρὸν δύνασθαι καὶ λόγον εἰς ἀνδρείας προσθήκην τοῖς ἀποδυομένοις πρὸς τὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς στάδιον. ΙΕʹ. Διὰ τοῦτο τῷ σώματι μὲν ἀπῆν, τῷ πνεύματι δὲ παρῆν, καὶ τοῖς ἀθλοῦσι συνηγωνίζετο· καὶ τῇ γλώσσῃ μὲν βοηθεῖν οὐκ εἶχεν, βοηθεῖ δὲ τῷ γράμ ματι. Πῶς; Ἀλείπτης ὑπερόριος γίνεται, τοὺς προτρεπτικοὺς συγγράφων, καὶ λογογραφῶν τὴν εὐσέβειαν, καὶ πλείους ἐκεῖνος σχεδὸν ἐξ ἐπι στολῶν ποιεῖται μάρτυρας μόνος, ἢ πάντες δι' ἑαυτῶν οἱ παρόντες τοῖς τότε κάμνουσι. Πείθει γὰρ, μὴ πατρίδα, μὴ γένος, μὴ περιουσίαν, μὴ δυναστείαν, μὴ ἄλλο τι τῶν χαμαὶ κειμένων, ἔμ προσθεν ἄγειν τῆς ἀληθείας, καὶ τῶν ἐκεῖθεν ἀποκειμένων ἄθλων τῆς ἀρετῆς, τοῖς ὑπὲρ τοῦ καλοῦ κινδυνεύουσι. Καὶ ταύτην εἶναι πραγματειῶν τὴν ἀρίστην, αἵματος ὀλίγου βασιλείαν οὐρα νῶν ὠνήσασθαι, καὶ δόξης ἀϊδιότητα τῶν προσ καίρων ἀντιλαβεῖν ἀγαθῶν. Μίαν μὲν γὰρ εἶναι πατρίδα τοῖς ὑψηλοῖς, τὴν νοουμένην Ἱερουσαλὴμ, οὐ τὰς μικροῖς ὁρίοις ἐνταῦθα διειλημμένας, καὶ πολλοὺς ἀμειβούσας οἰκήτορας· μίαν δὲ γένους λαμπρότητα, τὴν τῆς εἰκόνος τήρησιν, καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἀρχέτυπον ἐξομοίωσιν, ὅσον ἐφικτὸν τοῖς σαρ κὸς δεσμίοις, καὶ βραχεῖαν ἀποῤῥοὴν τοῦ καλοῦ δέχεσθαι δυναμένοις· μίαν δὲ δυναστείαν, τὸ κατὰ τοῦ πονηροῦ κράτος, καὶ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀνάλωτον καὶ ἀήττητον ἐν τοῖς ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας ἀγῶσιν, ἡνίκα κακία πρὸς ἀρετὴν ἀγωνίζεται, καὶ κόσμος πρὸς κόσμον, ὁ λυόμενος πρὸς τὸν ἑστῶ τα, καὶ πικρὸς ἀγωνοθέτης πρὸς γενναίους ἀγωνιστὰς, καὶ Βελίαρ πρὸς Χριστὸν παρατάσσεται. Διὰ ταῦτα καταφρονεῖν μὲν ξιφῶν ἀνέ πειθε, ψυχρὸν δὲ νομίζειν τὸ πῦρ, ἡμέρους δὲ οἴεσθαι θηρῶν τοὺς ἀγριωτάτους, λιμὸν δὲ ὑπο λαμβάνειν τὴν ἀνωτάτω τρυφὴν, δάκρυα δὲ τῶν οἰκείων, καὶ θρήνους, καὶ οἰμωγὰς παρατρέχειν, ὡς τοῦ πονηροῦ δελεάσματα, καὶ κωλύματα τῆς θείας ὁδοιπορίας. Ταῦτα γὰρ εἶναι ἀνδρικῶν ψυχῶν καὶ γενναίων, καὶ λογισμοῦ σώφρονος. Καὶ τὸ παράδειγμα ἐγγύθεν αὐτὸς ὁ ταῦτα λέγων καὶ γρά φων, πάντα ἡγησάμενος σκύβαλα, ἵνα Χριστὸν κερδήσῃ. Ιςʹ. Οὕτω διανοούμενος Κυπριανὸς, καὶ οὕτως ὁπλίζων τοῖς λόγοις πρὸς τὸν ἀγῶνα, πολλοὺς ἀθλητὰς ἀπειργάζετο. Καὶ τίνα μισθὸν τούτων κο μίζεται; Ὡς δαψιλῆ καὶ φιλότιμον! Μάρτυς ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἷς προέπεμψε γίνεται, ξίφει τὴν κεφαλὴν τμηθεὶς καὶ ταῖς πολλαῖς βασάνοις ταύτην ἐπιτίθησι τὴν κορωνίδα.
thought_title: Cyprian makes martyrs by letter from exile
orientation: Gregory shows how Decius exiled Cyprian to silence him, and how Cyprian still strengthened the persecuted by letters until his beheading.
pass_a_gloss: For by as much as he knew the man to excel in piety and in reputation, by so much he saw the victory for himself to be more conspicuous and more splendid, if he should master him. For in the one way it was to master Christians only, but in the other way it was to master philosophy itself, and words. And to remove the tongue first, then to lead away speechless and without reason those supported by it, he judged to be best generalship; planning these things not rightly nor piously, yet not altogether without reckoning, at least toward his own wish and undertaking; and the deed showed it. For after he shook off every assault and trial manfully and nobly, as a rock by the sea shakes off the onrushes of waves, at last he is condemned by him to exile; the noble man did not cherish what concerned himself, nor did he love being kept safe; nor did he judge safety for the body to be dishonor, and quiet to be danger for the soul, and to overlook the others being endangered at the crisis, when there is no trainer and no one emboldening toward the contest. For it is not a small thing to be able also by word to add to courage for those stripping for the stadium of virtue. 15. For this reason in body he was absent, but in spirit he was present, and he contended together with those contending; and with the tongue he had no means to help, but he helps with the letter. How? He becomes an anointer beyond the border, composing exhortations, and writing piety in prose, and he alone by letters makes almost more martyrs than all those present by themselves make among those then laboring. For he persuades those being endangered for the noble cause to lead before truth, and before the prizes of virtue laid up yonder, neither fatherland, nor birth, nor wealth, nor power, nor any other thing of the things lying on the ground. And that this is best of business, to buy kingship of heavens with little blood, and to receive in exchange eternity of glory for temporary good things. For there is one fatherland for the lofty, the Jerusalem apprehended by mind, not those here divided by small boundaries and exchanging many inhabitants; and one splendor of birth, the guarding of the image, and likening to the archetype, as far as is possible for prisoners of flesh and for those able to receive a small outflow of the noble; and one power, the mastery against the evil one, and the unconsumed and unconquered state of the soul in contests for piety, when vice contends against virtue, and world against world, the dissolving against the standing, and a bitter judge of the contest against noble champions, and Beliar arrayed against Christ. For these reasons he persuaded to despise swords, and to judge fire to be cold, and to suppose the wildest beasts to be tame, and to take hunger to be highest luxury, and to run past tears of kinsmen, and lamentations, and wailings, as baits of the evil one and hindrances of the divine journey. For these things belong to manly and noble souls and to sober reckoning. And the example was near, he himself who says and writes these things, having judged all things refuse, in order to gain Christ. 16. So thinking, Cyprian, and so arming with words toward the contest, made many athletes. And what reward for these things does he carry off? How lavish and generous! He becomes martyr after all whom he sent forward, having been cut as to the head with a sword, and upon his many torments he places this crown.

choices.why: brief glossary requires philosophy for the Christian way of life, not a paraphrase
keeps contest image of one who oils athletes, and literal sense of exile
literal sense of worthless waste in the quoted claim to gain Christ
brief glossary requires champion for one who fights for the truth
cast gives Beliar as name for the devil arrayed against Christ

bible_refs.note: πάντα ἡγησάμενος σκύβαλα, ἵνα Χριστὸν κερδήσῃ

pass_b_english: For the more Decius recognized how far Cyprian excelled in devotion and renown, the more conspicuous and brilliant he judged his own victory would be if he mastered him. In the one course he would master only Christians, but in the other he would master philosophy itself and eloquence. To cut out the tongue first, and then to carry off voiceless and speechless those who leaned on it, seemed to him the finest strategy. He reasoned in this unjust and impious way, yet not entirely without calculation for his own desire and enterprise. And events proved it.

For after Cyprian had shaken off every attack and trial with courage and nobility, like a sea cliff shaking off the rush of waves, at last Decius condemned him to exile. The noble man did not cling to his own concerns, nor did he love being kept safe. He did not reckon disgrace as safety for the body so much as quiet, and watching others face danger in the crisis, as danger to the soul, with no trainer to train them and embolden them for the contest. For speech added to courage is no small help to those who strip for the stadium of virtue.

So he was absent in body but present in spirit, and he contended alongside those in the contest. He could no longer help with his tongue, but he helps with his pen. How? He becomes an anointer beyond the border, writing letters of encouragement and composing works in defense of devotion, and almost single-handedly he makes more martyrs through his letters than all those present in person made among the sufferers of that time. He persuades those who risk their lives for what is good to put neither homeland nor family nor wealth nor power nor any other earthly thing before the truth and the prizes of virtue laid up above. This, he says, is the finest business, to buy the kingdom of heaven with a little blood and to receive eternal glory in exchange for passing goods.

For there is one homeland for the exalted, the Jerusalem of the mind, not the lands here divided by narrow boundaries and changing their many inhabitants. There is one splendor of birth, to guard the image and to become like the archetype as far as is possible for prisoners of the flesh who can receive only a slight outflow of the good. There is one power, might against the evil one and a soul unconsumed and undefeated in the contests for devotion, when vice contends against virtue and world against world, the dissolving against the standing, and the bitter judge of the contest against noble champions, and Beliar is arrayed against Christ. For these reasons he urged them to despise swords and to count fire as cold, to reckon the wildest beasts as tame and to regard the highest luxury as hunger, and to run past the tears and laments and wailings of their kin as lures of the evil one and hindrances on the divine journey. These responses belong to courageous and noble souls and to self-controlled reason. And the example stood close at hand in the man himself who spoke and wrote these things, who counted all things as refuse in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:8).

With this mind Cyprian armed many for the contest by his words and made them athletes. And what payment does he receive for this work? How rich and generous it is! He becomes a martyr after all those he sent ahead, beheaded by the sword, and upon his many tortures he sets this crown.
notes: source has spaced printing in κρατή σειεν, διανοού μενος, γράμ ματι, ἐπι στολῶν, ἔμ προσθεν, οὐρα νῶν, προσ καίρων, σαρ κὸς, ἑστῶ τα, ἀνέ πειθε, ὑπο λαμβάνειν, γρά φων, κο μίζεται; read as single words; section numbers 15 and 16 mark divisions

problems.quote: He did not count bodily safety as safety, but as disgrace, and quiet as danger to the soul, along with watching others face danger in the crisis
problems.source_quote: οὐδὲ ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι μᾶλλον τὴν ἀτιμίαν ἐνόμιζεν, ἢ ψυχῆς κίνδυνον τὴν ἡσυχίαν, καὶ τὸ περιορᾷν τοὺς ἄλλους
problems.why: The pairs are reversed: he refuses to treat disgrace as bodily safety, and instead treats quiet and neglecting others as danger to the soul.
problems.fix: Nor did he reckon disgrace as safety for the body rather than quiet—and watching others face the crisis with no trainer—as danger to the soul.
problems.ruling: Source has ἀσφάλειαν…τὴν ἀτιμίαν (disgrace as safety) in a οὐδὲ…μᾶλλον…ἢ comparison. English reverses it to 'safety as disgrace' and drops the comparison.

edits.old: He did not count bodily safety as safety, but as disgrace, and quiet as danger to the soul, along with watching others face danger in the crisis with no trainer to train them and embolden them for the contest.
edits.new: He did not reckon disgrace as safety for the body so much as quiet as danger to the soul, along with watching others face danger in the crisis with no trainer to train them and embolden them for the contest.

fixed: Fixed safety/disgrace reversal: source has ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι as predicate and τὴν ἀτιμίαν as object, matched by ψυχῆς κίνδυνον predicate with τὴν ἡσυχίαν object under μᾶλλον... ἢ, so disgrace refused as bodily safety and quiet taken as soul-danger.

problems.quote: He did not reckon disgrace as safety for the body so much as quiet as danger to the soul, along with watching others face danger
problems.source_quote: οὐδὲ ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι μᾶλλον τὴν ἀτιμίαν ἐνόμιζεν, ἢ ψυχῆς κίνδυνον τὴν ἡσυχίαν
problems.why: The comparison is garbled and hard to follow. The sense is that he counted dishonourable exile less a safety for the body than quiet a danger to the soul, and likewise standing by while others faced danger.
problems.fix: He did not count the dishonour of exile as safety for the body so much as he counted quiet a danger to his soul, and likewise standing idly by while others faced danger in this crisis.
problems.ruling: μᾶλλον…ἤ is lost: ἀτιμίαν is not bodily ἀσφάλειαν more than ἡσυχίαν is ψυχῆς κίνδυνον; the English comparison is unreadable.

fixed: Fixed garbled comparison to match source οὐδὲ ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι μᾶλλον τὴν ἀτιμίαν ἐνόμιζεν, ἢ ψυχῆς κίνδυνον τὴν ἡσυχίαν, καὶ τὸ περιορᾷν: both quiet and watching others are reckoned as danger to the soul.

problems.quote: to take hunger as the highest feast
problems.source_quote: λιμὸν δὲ ὑπολαμβάνειν τὴν ἀνωτάτω τρυφήν
problems.why: The predicate is λιμόν, parallel to 'fire as cold' and 'beasts as tame'. The sense is to count the highest luxury as hunger. The English reverses it.
problems.fix: and to regard the highest luxury as hunger
problems.ruling: Articular τὴν ἀνωτάτω τρυφήν is the object, anarthrous λιμόν the predicate, as with ψυχρὸν…τὸ πῦρ: reckon supreme luxury as hunger. English swaps them.

fixed: Fixed hunger/luxury reversal: λιμὸν (predicate) ... τὴν ἀνωτάτω τρυφὴν (object) parallels ψυχρὸν ... τὸ πῦρ, so luxury is counted as hunger.

Left exile sentence unchanged as correct: ἀσφάλειαν (predicate) ... τὴν ἀτιμίαν (object) with μᾶλλον ... ἢ = not so much...as, and τὸ περιορᾷν sharing ψυχῆς κίνδυνον; safety-to-dishonor reading reverses article pattern.

refereed.quote: He did not reckon disgrace as safety for the body so much as quiet, and watching others face danger in the crisis, as danger to the soul, with no trainer to train them
refereed.source_quote: οὐδὲ ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι μᾶλλον τὴν ἀτιμίαν ἐνόμιζεν, ἢ ψυχῆς κίνδυνον τὴν ἡσυχίαν, καὶ τὸ περιορᾷν τοὺς ἄλλους τῷ καιρῷ κινδυνεύοντας
refereed.why: The comparison is scrambled. The source says he counted quiet and watching others in danger a greater peril to his soul than disgrace is a safety for his body. The English is hard to follow and the logic is unclear.
refereed.fix: He did not count the disgrace of exile as safety for his body, but counted quiet, and looking on while others faced danger at such a time, as peril to his soul, with no trainer to embolden them for the contest.
refereed.ruling: οὐδὲ ἀσφάλειαν τῷ σώματι μᾶλλον τὴν ἀτιμίαν…ἢ ψυχῆς κίνδυνον τὴν ἡσυχίαν: English breaks which item is body-safety versus soul-danger.
